50 YEARS IN PSI UPSILON
THIS
is the story of three Delta men who have just celebrated the
fiftieth anniversary of their initiation into Psi Upsilon.
In September 1879 James Abbott, Charles Lawrence Bristol and
William Morgan Kingsley entered as freshmen in the class of 1883 in New
York University.
On December 16, 1879, we were initiated into the Delta Chapter.
There is nothing remarkable about this statement, but what follows
we believe establishes a record. We have held an annual reunion on or
about December 16 of each year since then and two of us have never been
absent from the celebration. The third one, Brother Bristol, was so far away
because of his professional duties that he could not be present. For a few
years he was kept in the far west and once on a cruise around the world, and
in December was in Japan. At no time was anyone absent on account of
illness.
As undergraduates we did the usual things that would be expected of us;
we held the usual offices in college and in the chapter, and in the senior year
each was for one term the "head of the house." In the senior year each was
elected to Phi Beta Kappa and on
graduation we were each commencement
orators. Brother Kingsley being Greek Salutatorian�
second honor. We
never missed any good times as students but we kept in favor with the faculty.
In time we all married and we each have a Psi U son.
On graduation Brother Bristol began his career as teacher and for 37
years was Professor of Biology in New York University being retired because
he had reached the age limit. He graduated with the degrees of B.S. and M.S.
and received from the University of Chicago the degree of Ph.D.
Brother Kingsley has been in Wall Street since 1883 and is now and has
been for several years the President of the U. S. Trust Co. of New York, and
is still going strong. He graduated with B.A. and M.A. and later as a
recognition of distinguished services, an appreciative board of trustees of New
York University bestowed upon him the honorary degree of L.L. D.
Brother Abbott entered The Century Company, publishers, in 1883 and as
an officer and head of a department worked there for 43 years, he also being
retired because of the age limit. He graduated with B.A. and has no other
academic degrees. As a graduate, Brother Kingsley served for 17 years on the
Executive Council of the Fratemity. He was chairman of a committee which
formed the New York Psi Upsilon Alumni Association from which grew the

We were all delegates to the Semi-Centennial Convention of Psi Upsilon
in Albany in May 1883 and it is our
expectation and ambition to attend the
centennial in 1933 and then to be present at the one hundredth anniversary
of the Delta in 1937. It seems eminently fitting that after fifty years service
in the Delta we shold celebrate there our golden anniversary. So on December
16, 1929, we met there almost to the hour of the ceremony of the initiation of
1879. With the chapter in meeting assembled and with the graduate Delta
men around us, we recalled old times and old faces and closed a long vista
of years with the Dear Old Shrine.
We have had our shortcomings and have made mistakes but we have never
been lacking in our loyalty to the Delta, nor in our allegiance to Psi Upsilon.

THETA THETA CHAPTER HONORS
A. P. SAWYER, BETA '80
IN
LASTING tribute to his long devotion to Psi Upsilon, and to his in
spiring leadership in the fraternity in the Pacific Northwest, Alumni
Brothers of the Theta Theta have presented to the undergraduate chap
ter an oil painting of Brother A. P. Sawyer, Beta, '80. The presentation
was made the principal Psi U. event of the University of Washington's
annual homecoming, and was attended by a large gathering of brothers from
many cities of Washington, Oregon and British Columbia, who came to
Seattle to participate. Brother Merville W. Mclnnis, Theta Theta, as chair
man of the committee in charge, presided.
The address of presentation was made by Brother W. H. Hutchinson,
of the Theta Theta, who eloquently expressed the affection of the brothers
of that chapter, and of all Psi U. men of this section, for the man who has
been so largely responsible for the establishment of the chapter at Washing
ton, and for its subsequent success.
The gift was accepted by Brother Reed Ingham, of the undergraduate
chapter. Brother David Whitcomb, of the Gamma, was called upon to pay
a tribute to Brother Sawyer's services to the fraternity, and particularly to
the part which he took in bringing Psi U. to Seattle. The high point of
the evening came when Brother Sawyer was asked to relate some of his
adventures as an exponent of the old Phi Kappa Society, which later became
the Theta Theta chapter. Brother Sawyer responded with his inimitable
wit and with his own graphic narrative style.
It seems superfluous to relate here that Brother Sawyer was one of
the first of the Psi U. Brothers of the Pacific Northwest to sense the fact
that the University of Washington had qualities suitable for the establishment
of a chapter of Psi Upsilon. Having become satisfied of this, he gave un
sparingly of his time and energy for over seven years, attending virtually
every convention during that period, and working in many other ways, to
bring a second chapter of the fraternity to the Pacific Coast. Since the
installation of that chapter, he has been the chapter's constant source of
inspiration and beloved guide.
The portrait which depicts Brother Sawyer in a characteristic pose, has
been hung in the chapter house of the Theta Theta, where brothers of that
chapter for generations to come will know it as an inspiration of devotion
to the fraternity. Mathew O'Connor

BY
HIS SELECTION of Senator Frederic M. Sackett, of Kentucky,
to be Ambassador to Germany, President Hoover has filled the three
highest American diplomatic posts, and two of the assignments have
gone to members of the senate. The Kentucky Senator, who is now on a rest
trip to Cuba, is expected to take over the Berlin office just vacated by Ambas
sador Schurman at an early date.
native of RHODE ISLAND
Although German officials declined to discuss selection of an American
ambassador, the early editions of German papers accepted appointment
of Senator Sackett as definite. "Der Montag" said that President Hoover
"chose a personality with a thorough economic and financial experience,
since the special status of the United States arising from the conclusion of
separate German-American reparation agreements demand at the Berlin post
a self-reliant and resourceful man on economic questions." The newspaper
expresses great surprise at the choice of Senator Sackett, although it said it
was known that the President intended to select a member of his war-time
relief organization.
It was the belief of Senator Sackett that business men should be willing
to give part of their time and ability to public service, and exemplifying
that belief, he served in municipal and State offices in Kentucky and the
United States Senate, notwithstanding that his diversified business interests
were sufficient to occupy all of his time. Senator Sackett, a native of Rhode
Island, went to Columbus, Ohio, shortly after receiving his law degree from
the Harvard Law School and practiced his profession in the Ohio capital for
four years. He then practiced in Cincinnati for a year and took up his
residence in Louisville in 1898.
Two years later he became interested in the coal industry, meanwhile
continuing his legal practice until 1907, when he virtually abandoned the
profession to devote his time to business. From 1907 to 1912 he was
president of the Louisville Gas Company and the Louisville Lighting Com
pany. He was then chosen president of the Pioneer and Black Star Coal
Companies, and vice president of the North Jellicoe and Beaver Dam Coal
Companies, the Louisville Cement Company and the Speed Realty Company.
The senator's interests also embraced banking, and he was a director of

DR. WILLIAM G. THAYER RESIGNS AS
HEADMASTER AT ST. MARK'S
The Rev. Dr. William Greenough Thayer, Gamma' 85, headmaster of
St. Mark's school for the past 36 years, tendered his resignation to the board
of trustees a few weeks ago, to become effective next September.
"Thirty-six years is a long span of time," he said. "I feel that I need
a rest."
If his resignation is accepted, he will also resign the rectorship of St.
Mark's Episcopal Church, which he has held for many years. His home at
present is at the school.
The news of his action was received with great concern and regret by
the town of Southboro, Mass., where he has played a
prominent part both
in social and civic affairs. The resignation was taken under advisement
and the board of trustees will report shortly.
Dr. Thayer was born at New Brighton, Staten Island, N. Y., Dec. 24,
1863, the son of Robert H. and Hannah (Appleton) Thayer. He was
graduated from Amherst College in 1885 and three years later received his
master's degree from that institution. After graduation he studied at Union
Theological Seminary and at the Episcopal Theological school at Cambridge.
Columbia University awarded him the honorary degree of master of
arts in 1906 and Amherst College in 1907 gave him the honorary degree of
doctor of divinity. After several years of teaching, including five years
as a member of the faculty at Groton school, he became headmaster of St.
Mark's in 1894. He became a deacon in 1889 and in the following year was
ordained a priest of the Episcopal church.
He served as
president of the standing committee of the diocese of
Massachusetts from 1910 until 1919, as a
delegate to the Republican state
convention of 1904, as a member of the co-operating committee of the war
council of the Y. M. C. A., as chairman of the diocesan committee on camps
and as a delegate to the general convention of the Protestant Episcopal
church in 1922.
In 1891 he married Violet Otis of Boston. They have seven children.

REINALD WERRENRATH, DELTA '05
NAMED VOCAL SUPERVISOR OF
NATIONAL BROADCASTING CO.
REINALD
WERRENRATH, America's most prominent baritone, has
been named vocal supervisor of NBC, to direct the vocal ensembles
, and soloists in the radio presentations of the chain. He is also
Musical Director of Psi Upsilon and is now visiting our chapters in this
responsibility. He is also planning to make some records of our songs
this year.
Under the terms of his new contract he will be heard on the air only
through the company's network, and his advice and counsel will apply to the
programs as a whole. This will not prohibit him, however, from making
personal appearances at concerts.
His work will parallel that of Walter Damrosch, who is musical counsel,
and has supervision of all symphonic and other instrumental presentations.
In speaking of his new post, Werrenrath said, "It is quite pleasing to hear
the clap-clap of a thousand hands, but it is far more interesting to get a
letter from a listener a thousand miles away who liked a song because it cre
ated a picture or developed a certain emotional reaction.
"I really believe you get as close to the people through the microphone as
you do from the concert stage, even though the actual distance between
the singer and the audience is far greater. There is the fascination of
going right into homes and appealing to people without the customary the
atrical effects; and the knowledge that if you aren't good they'll tune you out
gives zest to the job.
"No sensible person will deny that radio is playing a
greater part each
year in the musical education and cultural development of America. It is a
great privilege to be in a
position to help a little in that development."
Werrenrath was born in Brooklyn and studied singing under his father,
George Werrenrath, and such noted musicians as Dr. Carl Dufft, Frank
King Clark, Dr. Arthur Mees, Percy Rector Stephens and Victor Maurel.
He made his operatic debut at the Metropolitan Opera House Feb. 19,
1919, as Sylvio in "I'Pagliacci." His career in concerts and oratorios was
begun in 1907 and he has been heard frequently in radio broadcasts during
the last few years.

CHESTER A. ARTHUR, THETA '48,
SECOND TO TAKE OATH IN NEW YORK
AS PRESIDENT
BURNSIDES
were a badge of sartorial distinction and bicycling was
a favorite sport with the country's elite when Vice President Chester
A. Arthur, New York lawyer and handsome widower, succeeded the
assassinated Garfield as President of the United States.
Requested by fhe cabinet to assume the presidency immediately after
Garfield's death, Gen. Arthur took the oath of office in the parlor of his
home at 123 Lexington avenue. New York City, at 2:20 o'clock the morning
of Sept. 20, 1881. He was the second of the Presidents to be sworn in at
New York, Washington's first inauguration taking place in old Federal hall.
ELIHU ROOT WAS THERE
Elihu Root witnessed the induction of Arthur. At the conclusion of
the simple ceremony, the general's 17-year-old son, Alan, Lambda '85, ap
proached his father, laying one arm on his shoulder, kissed him. Two days
later, President Arthur again took the oath at the capitol in the presence of
members of the cabinet, senators and other government dignitaries. For the
first time in history, two ex-Presidents, Grant and Hayes, were at the ceremony.
The nation was in mourning for Garfield and there were no inaugural
festivities or social events at the White House for several months.
Six feet tall, broad shouldered and handsome, President Arthur was
described as "a man of courtly bearing, fine dress and artistic tastes." A
contemporary wrote: "In Gen. Arthur we have a new type of man in the
White House. There have been Presidents of all kinds. We have had
stately Virginia gentlemen of the old school and self-made men from the
west.

WHISKERS WERE POPULAR
On Sept. 27, 1881, the name of Kalakaua Rex, "his olive-tinted majesty
of the Sandwich isles," adorned the register of the Arlington hotel in
Washington. Even in that era of hirsute glory in America, his majesty
was the envy of the Beau Brummels at the capital. Setting off his brown
skin, he had black, curly hair and sported a mustache, goatee and side
whiskers. When he called on President Arthur he wore a "plain black
suit, plug hat and boiled shirt besides displaying other emblems of con
tinental civilization."
"The thorny questions of social precedence again arose under this
administration," says Esther Singleton in her "Story of the White House."
The President was a widower and his little daughter, Nellie, was too young
to do the honors of the White House. His sister, Mrs. McElroy, presided
on most occasions.
LADIES VIE FOR PLACE

New Year's day, and heart burning and jealousies naturally arose as to
who should take the stand of honor on his immediate right. The vexed
question was immediately decided by him in favor of the claim of the wife
of the speaker of the house in accordance with what he considered the strict
rules of official precedence."

PSI UPSILON RANKS FIRST IN SCHOLAR
SHIP AT SYRACUSE UNIVERSITY
FORMAL
announcement has been made, through the Registrar's Office,
of Syracuse University of the scholarship ratings of the 32 social
fraternities. The report this year shows that many changes have
taken place in the standings of the fratemities since 1927-1928.
Psi Upsilon has jumped from ninth place to take first, which has been
held by Acacia for the past two years. The former leaders have fallen to
18th position this year, while Gamma Eta Gamma retained its hold on the
second place.
ALPHA PHI DELTA TAKES THIRD.
The rise of Alpha Phi Delta from 32 to third is very noteworthy, as was
that of Delta Upsilon from 22nd to fourth. Sigma Alpha Mu again held
its place among the first five this year.
The highest average for last year was 1.301, while for 1927-1928 it
was 1.442. The low average was .714 as
compared to .685 of the previous
year. Taking both years into consideration the averages for the past year
show a slight increase over that of the proceeding year.
WOMEN RATE HIGHER THAN MEN.
When compared with the averages of the sororities the rating of the
men shows a great difference. Alpha Epsilon Phi was high among the
women with 1.662, while the low was 1.042.
Seven of the first ten fraternities for 1927-1928 have fallen to lower
places. Alpha Sigma Phi and Kappa Sigma, who were fourth and fifth,
are in 25th and 13th places this year. While Zeta Psi, Theta Chi, Lambda
Chi Alpha, and Phi Gamma Delta have gone from sixth, seventh, eighth and
tenth to 23, 24, 19, and 21, respectively.
Before making up the final rating each fraternity was sent a copy of
the grades of each student belonging to that house, showing the hours passed,
grade points made and those deducted for the past two semesters. Each
fraternity was allowed to make any corrections before the final data was
tabulated.�

ACHIEVING THE IMPOSSIBLE.
In raising its chapter scholastic standing from practically the bottom
of the interfraternity list to first place within two years' time, Psi Upsilon
achieved what was considered the impossible. The fraternity, as a whole,
is to be highly congratulated for an entirely successful effort in improving
its internal scholastic condition.
For a number of years Acacia has shown its heels to the rest of
Syracuse's fraternities. Each time the statistics disclosed the fact that the
Masonic organization was on top, the other Hill Greeks merely agreed that
the expected had happened, and as a result, thought nothing of it.
But not so with Psi Upsilon. The chapter officers simply considered
the task of dislodging Acacia a possible one and set out to do the job. Last
year the residents of the huge yellow mansion overlooking the campus
bettered their position considerably. This year the ratings show that Psi
Upsilon heads the list.
The campus, as a whole, extends heartiest congratulations. May the
other chapters improve their own standings by following the example set
by the local organization of Psi Upsilon.�

Scholastic Averages
On January 8, formal announcement was made through the office of the
Registrar of the scholastic averages of the 32 fraternities.
The scholastic averages are based on the count system. In this
3 points are awarded for each credit hour with grade of A.
2 points are awarded for each credit hour with grade of B.
1 point is awarded for each credit hour with grade of C.
0 points are awarded for each credit hour with grade of D,
E, or F.
Counts for each course constitute the number of credit hours added to
the number of points.
Grades of E and F receive no credit hours.
Averages are obtained by dividing the number of counts obtained by
the total number of credit hours taken.
One point is deducted for each class cut over twelve, and also for every
cut taken within forty-eight hours of a vacation.
During 1928-1929 the average was taken on the active chapter, which
included 58 men. Point deductions totaled 56 for overcuts in that same
period, of which 37 were taken by three men.

ON

UPSILON CHAPTER is going through one of the most important

balance will be raised from Alumni who have not yet responded.
To offset a
tendency toward delinquency among undergraduates in pay
ment of dues and house accounts, we have inaugurated a system under which
each parent, or responsible guardian, of a man about to be initiated is
advised of the approximate financial responsibility entailed by the boy in
entering the fraternity. The parent is requested to sign and return to the
Treasurer a statement to the effect that he will make good any delinquency
in the man's account on ten days' written notice, if the account is as much
as thirty days overdue. This plan has worked very satisfactorily during the
past year, and has, to a large extent, prevented the diversion of allowances
by the parents to uses which were not intended.
The activities of the Campaign Committee for funds has created a new
and stronger interest on the part of all Alumni than has ever been shown.
This applies to Alumni of other chapters living in, and near, Rochester, as
